title: Tabs and sessions
one_line_goal: Many tabs, restored after a restart, with separate data per site
summary: Turn the single view into tabs: switching, shortcuts, restore after a crash, a profile per site, history, basic downloads, a settings screen and a sidebar.

tasks.title: Tab rules as plain code
tasks.what: The rules for tabs (open, close, switch, reorder, reopen a closed tab), written as plain code with no window attached.
tasks.why: Tab logic has many edge cases. Testing it without a window catches mistakes early: always one active tab, ids never reused.
tasks.how: Write the rules in the app's core code. Run normal tests plus tests that try random sequences of actions and check every rule still holds.
tasks.chain: Tab logic has many edge cases → write it without the window and test random sequences of actions → exactly one active tab, ids never reused.
tasks.check: Unit and random-sequence tests keep every rule.

tasks.title: One web view per tab
tasks.what: Each tab gets its own website view: hidden or shown when you switch, resized with the window, fully closed with the tab.
tasks.why: Tabs must not freeze the app or leave processes running after they close.
tasks.how: Create views only from non-blocking code (blocking code freezes on Windows), hide and show them on switch, release everything on close. A test opens and closes 20 tabs.
tasks.chain: Each tab needs its own view → create views only from non-blocking code, hide and show on switch, release fully on close → no freezes or leftover processes.
tasks.check: Open 20 tabs, switch, close all: view count back to zero, no leftover processes.

tasks.title: Tab strip and shortcuts
tasks.what: A tab strip plus keyboard shortcuts for new tab, close tab, next and previous tab, address bar, back, forward and reload.
tasks.why: Shortcuts must work even while you are inside a website, without giving websites any access to the app.
tasks.how: Handle the shortcuts in the trusted shell. The exact way to catch keys while a website has focus is not checked yet; this phase checks it.
tasks.chain: Shortcuts must work even while typing in a website → handle them in the shell without giving websites access → fast and still safe.
tasks.check: Each shortcut works from the shell and from a tab; the bridge lockdown test still passes.

tasks.title: Saved settings and startup sites
tasks.what: A saved settings file, including the websites that open at startup.
tasks.why: Settings must survive crashes and app upgrades, so they are never lost or half-written.
tasks.how: A versioned file in the app's config folder, written to a temporary file and then swapped in, with an upgrade path. A damaged file falls back to defaults and keeps a backup.
tasks.chain: Settings must survive crashes and upgrades → a versioned file, written safely, with migration → never lost or half-written.
tasks.check: Round trip works; a future version is refused clearly; a corrupt file falls back with a backup; startup sites open in order.

tasks.title: Restore tabs after restart or crash
tasks.what: Your tabs (address, order, active tab, profile, place in history) come back after a restart or a crash.
tasks.why: Crashes happen. After a forced kill you should still get your tabs back.
tasks.how: Save the tab list regularly and on exit, writing a temporary file and then renaming it, so a crash never leaves a half-written file. Restore it on start.
tasks.chain: Crashes happen → save the tab list regularly and on exit, safely → after a forced kill you get your tabs back.
tasks.check: Normal exit, forced kill and unreachable-site restores all behave.

tasks.title: Separate profile per site
tasks.what: Per-site settings, including which separate profile (data store) each site uses.
tasks.why: Sites should not see each other's cookies and stored data.
tasks.how: Assign profiles through the route chosen in P1. Decide and write down what counts as one site: the exact web address origin or the wider domain.
tasks.chain: Sites should not see each other's data → assign profiles using the route chosen in P1 → cookies stay apart.
tasks.check: Two sites in different profiles cannot see each other's cookies; one site in two tabs shares one profile; survives restart.

tasks.title: History
tasks.what: Back and forward for each tab, plus a list of the pages you visited.
tasks.why: History is useful but private: it stays on this PC, can be cleared, and never goes into the project files.
tasks.how: Keep back and forward per tab in the shell and the visit list in a local file. A test checks that clearing empties both the list and the file.
tasks.chain: You need back/forward per tab and a list of visited pages → kept locally, clearable, never in the repo → useful without leaking.
tasks.check: History tests pass; clearing empties the list and the file.

tasks.title: Basic downloads
tasks.what: Basic downloads: save to the Downloads folder or ask where, and show progress, completion and errors.
tasks.why: Files must land somewhere sensible, and you must see what happened to them.
tasks.how: Use the app framework's download hook. Stricter download safety rules come later, in P4.
tasks.chain: Files must land somewhere sensible → default folder or a prompt, with progress and errors → downloads are visible.
tasks.check: A test file arrives with the right size and fingerprint; a failing one shows an error.

tasks.title: Shell stays responsive
tasks.what: A check that the browser stays usable while one tab is very busy.
tasks.why: A busy website must not freeze the whole browser.
tasks.how: A test page keeps one tab busy; switching tabs and typing must finish within a time limit. That busy tabs run apart from the shell is not checked yet; this checks it.
tasks.chain: A busy tab must not freeze the browser → switch tabs and type while another tab burns CPU → the shell stays usable.
tasks.check: Switching and typing finish within the test's time limit (a requirement, not a measurement).

tasks.title: Guard against the freeze bug
tasks.what: A guard that stops the known Windows freeze bug from coming back.
tasks.why: Creating tab views from blocking code freezes the app on Windows.
tasks.how: A code review checklist item, plus a test that creates tabs from the shell's command path in a loop and must finish without hanging.
tasks.chain: Creating views from blocking code freezes on Windows → make that path impossible and test it in a loop → the bug cannot come back.
tasks.check: A review checklist item plus a loop test that never hangs.

tasks.title: Settings screen
tasks.what: A settings screen in the trusted shell for startup sites, per-site settings with profiles, and the download folder.
tasks.why: You can change these without editing files, while websites still cannot touch your settings.
tasks.how: The screen reads and changes settings only through app commands that check the input and save safely. Bad input, like a missing folder, is refused.
tasks.chain: You need to change startup sites, profiles and the download folder → a settings screen in the trusted shell, checked by the app → websites still cannot touch settings.
tasks.check: Changes persist and apply after restart; bad input is refused; websites cannot call these commands.

tasks.title: Sidebar of tabs and history
tasks.what: A sidebar you can open and close, listing open tabs and your history.
tasks.why: Website views are always drawn on top of the shell, so anything placed over them would be hidden.
tasks.how: Place the sidebar beside the website area and shrink the tab view when it opens, so the two never overlap. A keyboard shortcut toggles it.
tasks.chain: Website views are always drawn over the shell → place the sidebar beside them, never on top → nothing is hidden or overlapped.
tasks.check: Toggling the sidebar resizes the tab view with no overlap; choosing an entry opens it.

tasks.title: One integration suite
tasks.what: One test suite combining the tests for tabs, restore, profiles, history, downloads, settings screen and sidebar.
tasks.why: One clean run is clear proof that the milestone works.
tasks.how: A single command runs the whole suite. It must finish with no failures, and its output is saved.
tasks.chain: Many features → one command runs every P3 test → a single green run proves the milestone.

tasks.title: Literature batch 3
tasks.what: A batch of reading: studies of how people use tabs, Chrome and Edge rules for sleeping tabs, and similar ideas on phones.
tasks.why: Tab lifecycle is the core research idea; this is the closest earlier work for P7.
tasks.how: Write dated research notes. Check the uncertain entries on the starting reading list, or keep them flagged.
tasks.chain: Tab lifecycle is the core research idea → read tab-usage studies and Chrome and Edge lifecycle policies → prior art for P7.
tasks.check: New dated notes; uncertain seed entries checked or still flagged.

tasks.title: Docs, gate, your review
tasks.what: Update the docs, run the phase gate and hand over for your review.
tasks.why: You decide when P3 is done, after using Ferrum for a real working session with many tabs.
tasks.how: Update part pages, the README features and known limits, save all evidence. Then you do the hand checks: eight or more tabs, shortcuts, kill and restore, a real download.
tasks.chain: Tabs done → update part pages, known limits and the README, then run the gate → you use Ferrum for a real working session and approve.
tasks.check: All evidence saved; wiki clean; you approved the P3 exit.

test_gate.explanation: Tabs multiply every P2 behaviour → rerun P2's tests plus the new suite, and test restore after a forced kill → you use it for a real working session → only then does security work start in P4.

rows.proves: Dependencies are allowed and have no open alerts.
Shell style, types and tests pass.
The app you would ship builds.
Tabs, restore, profiles, history, downloads, settings and sidebar work.
P2's quick app tests and the bridge lockdown still pass.
You used eight or more tabs, every shortcut, a kill-and-restore and a real download.
